name: Aisha Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior buyer at Harbourline Foodservice. We supply restaurants, care homes and school kitchens, and I buy the dry goods: rice, flour, cooking oil, tinned tomatoes. I'm in by eight, I check what the warehouse says is running low, and I ring round the suppliers for prices. Most of my day is phone calls, purchase orders and chasing deliveries that didn't turn up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the suppliers, honestly. There's a man at the flour mill who knows my voice and always warns me when prices are about to jump. What wears me out is the new ordering system, which keeps suggesting quantities I don't trust, and Marion, my manager, says I'm the slowest on the team at clearing it. I've been here eighteen months and I still feel like I'm catching up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a lot of noise and not much else. At work I'd make a joke of it with the warehouse crew about the robots that never came. Online I'd post something about how the money went into tech firms instead of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even the small stuff worries me, because the routine stuff is my whole job. If the system gets a bit better at suggesting orders, Marion needs fewer people clearing it, and I'm the slowest one. Even if AI is mostly hype, it only has to replace the slowest buyer at my firm, and right now that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing it my way, phoning the suppliers from my notebook, because that's what keeps the prices right. I'd cut what I can at home, the streaming and the Friday takeaway with Dev, because our rent went up again in September. And I'd talk to Kev, the union rep in the warehouse, about whether office staff like me can join.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not a disaster picture, but I'm already one bad month from not making rent, so nothing changing isn't the same as being fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're one bad month from not making rent. What does a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad month is Dev's hours getting cut on the bus routes, or the car needing a repair. We've got maybe three weeks of money saved. Last winter the boiler went and I borrowed from my mum, and I hated asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the union, rather than just working faster on the system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'll never be the fastest on a screen; I know that about myself. The warehouse crew got a pay rise last year because they stood together, and nobody in the office got anything. If the system is going to be used to measure us, I'd rather there's someone in the room who's on our side.

say: AI turned out to be **mostly noise**, just like I expected.
The money went into **tech firms** instead of into people's wages.
think: Even small automation hits me, because **routine ordering** is most of my working day.
A smarter system means Marion needs **fewer people**, and I'm the **slowest** at clearing it.
do: Keep phoning suppliers from my **paper notebook**, because that's how I get good prices.
Cut the **streaming** and the Friday takeaway, since our rent rose again in September.
Ask Kev, the warehouse **union rep**, whether office staff like me can join.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, because I'm already one bad month from **missing rent**.
S0.quote: Even if AI is mostly hype, it only has to replace the slowest buyer at my firm, and right now that's me.
fieldNote: Her worry **predates AI**: three weeks of savings, a rent rise and a partner on variable hours.
She treats even modest automation as a threat because she already **ranks last** on the new system.
Her instinct under pressure is **standing together**, not getting faster on screens.

steps.text: Keep phoning rice and flour suppliers from the paper notebook
Cancel the streaming subscription and the Friday takeaway
Ask the warehouse union rep about letting office buyers join

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need rules, so firms can't swap buyers for software without a plan for the people. I'd say it in the break room and I'd share the union posts online. I wouldn't be shy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying is right there on that list, and I think my job goes. Not straight away, but the firm won't replace people when they leave, and a junior who doesn't use the tools is the first one they stop needing. My manager will call it a restructure, and I'll be the buyer whose desk becomes a printer stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get the office people signed up with the warehouse union, properly, before the cuts come. I'd write to our council member about rules on job cuts and money for retraining. And I'd quietly ask the warehouse supervisor about picking jobs, because the robots are slower to get to the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. It's like watching the bus come and knowing it isn't stopping for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. If learning them could keep you in the job, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try if they made me; I'm not stupid about it. But I've seen how it goes: they train you for a week, then measure you against the people who were already quick. I'd rather put my effort into the floor job, where I know what good work looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The food shop moves to the discount store on River Road; that's first. Then the gym, which I barely use anyway. Dev and I had talked about a holiday next summer, and that would be the first thing we stop talking about.

say: Firms shouldn't swap buyers for software **without a plan** for the people.
This is exactly why office workers need **rules** and a **union** behind them.
think: Buying is on the list, and I expect **my job goes** within a few years.
A junior who **won't use the tools** is the first one the firm stops needing.
do: Sign up the office buyers with the **warehouse union** before any cuts are announced.
Write to our **council member** about rules on job cuts and retraining money.
Ask the supervisor about **picking jobs**, since robots reach the warehouse floor more slowly.
feel: **Sick**, like watching a bus come that isn't going to **stop for me**.
S1.quote: My manager will call it a restructure, and I'll be the buyer whose desk becomes a printer stand.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and reads the card's list as a description of her desk.
She would only learn AI tools **under orders**, and doubts training would save her anyway.
Her escape route is **downward into hands-on work**, which she trusts more than screens.

steps.text: Get the office buyers signed up with the warehouse union
Write to the council member about rules on job cuts
Ask the warehouse supervisor about a stock-picking job
Move the weekly food shop to the discount store

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in now, not in five years, with a wage for people whose jobs disappear. I'd be at whatever protest was happening in town. People would need to see it's not just a few office types complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't think I'd have a plan. My job is phone and screen work, so it goes in 2028, and the warehouse jobs only last till about 2031. In two years I'd go from buying rice for school kitchens to queuing at the job office with the cooks from those kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for anything hands-on straight away: warehouse, care homes, cleaning, because that's where the three extra years are. We'd live on Dev's wage while I looked, though driving buses isn't safe forever either. And I'd join the protests, because what else is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. My chest goes tight just thinking about it, because there's no money to buy time with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap feel like time, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years on a warehouse floor is something, I suppose. But everyone in my office would be chasing the same few floor jobs, and the warehouse only takes on two or three people a year. So it's time, but it's time for the people who get there first, and I'm never first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sorry, probably, which is silly because it isn't my fault. Then I'd ask him how long his routes are safe. We'd sit at the kitchen table and do sums we can't make work.

say: The government has to pay a **wage** to people whose jobs disappear, **starting now**.
I'd be at every **protest** in town, so people see it isn't just office workers moaning.
think: My phone and screen job **goes in 2028**, and I honestly wouldn't have a **plan**.
Warehouse work only lasts until **about 2031**, and everyone from the office would want it.
do: Apply straight away for **hands-on jobs** in warehouses, care homes and cleaning.
Live on **Dev's bus wage** while I look, knowing his job isn't safe either.
Join the **protests** in town, because there's nothing else I can see to do.
feel: **Panicky**, with a tight chest, because there's **no money** to buy time.
S2.quote: In two years I'd go from buying rice for school kitchens to queuing at the job office with the cooks from those kitchens.
fieldNote: With three weeks of savings and a resistant streak, she has **no plan** and says so plainly.
She sees the **three-year robot gap** as real but crowded, and expects to lose the race.
Her household rests on **one wage** that she also thinks is exposed.

steps.text: Live on Dev's bus driving wage while job hunting
Apply for warehouse, care home and cleaning jobs around town
Join protests in town calling for a wage for replaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get rules in place, so let's not waste them. I'd push the union to bargain for retraining money now, while the firm still needs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes it a bit, because I'd be thirty-two, and the floor work lasts until about 2034. My buying job still goes, I'm sure of that. But there's time to get a forklift licence or something with my hands before the AI arrives, if I can find the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the forklift course at the evening college next spring; it costs about the same as a month's food. I'd put forty a month aside, even if it means no takeaways at all. And I'd keep pushing at union meetings for the firm to pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but the kind of frightened where you can do something. Less like falling, more like a long drop you can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI tools. Would five years of warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd learn the basics, so I'm not lost. But I wouldn't bet my future on getting good at the thing that's replacing me. Getting good at the software that's replacing me would only help my firm replace me faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joyce, who's done the frozen buying for twenty years and is fifty-eight. She's brilliant on the phone and worse on the computer than me. She's too old to start on a forklift and too young to retire, and nobody's planning anything for people like Joyce.

say: We have **five years** to get rules in place, so we mustn't waste them.
The union should bargain for **retraining money** now, while the firm still needs us.
think: My **buying job** still goes, but I'd be thirty-two with time to switch.
A **forklift licence** before 2031 buys me floor work until about 2034.
do: Sign up for the **forklift course** at the evening college next spring.
Put **forty a month** aside, even if it means no takeaways at all.
Keep pushing at **union meetings** for the firm to pay for retraining.
feel: Still **frightened**, but it's a drop I can **see coming** and prepare for.
S3.quote: Getting good at the software that's replacing me would only help my firm replace me faster.
fieldNote: Five years turns her **panic into a plan**, though she still expects to lose the buying job.
She refuses to invest effort in AI tools, seeing them as **training her replacement**.
Her concern for Joyce, an older colleague, shows a strong sense of **who gets left behind**.

steps.text: Start a forklift licence at the evening college next spring
Put forty a month into a savings pot
Push at union meetings for firm-paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if the government actually uses it. Free retraining, rules on how fast firms can cut. I'd keep saying it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is different. I'd be thirty-seven, and that's a whole career change, not a panic. The buying still goes in 2036, but I could be well into something else by then, and robots for hands-on work wouldn't come until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Harbourline for now; there's no rush to leave a job that pays. Over the next couple of years I'd look for an apprenticeship, maybe electrical work or plumbing, where the robots are last to arrive. And I'd vote for whoever promises proper retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not sick. It's far enough off that I can sleep, and close enough that I know I can't just ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship on low pay, with less than a month saved. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't answer yet. We'd need Dev on full hours, and both of us cutting right back for a year or two. Maybe that's why ten years matters: it gives me time to save before I jump, instead of jumping with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said electrical or plumbing. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Ray's an electrician and he's never once been short of work. Nobody wants a robot poking around their fuse box at nine at night, and my uncle Ray has been doing that for thirty years.

say: **Ten years** is enough to do this properly, if the government actually uses it.
We need **free retraining** and rules on how fast firms can cut jobs.
think: At thirty-seven I'd be making a **career change**, not scrambling in a panic.
Robots for hands-on work wouldn't come **until about 2039**, which gives a trade real years.
do: Keep the **buying job** for now, since there's no reason to leave paid work early.
Look for an **electrical or plumbing** apprenticeship within the next couple of years.
Vote for whoever promises **proper retraining** money.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to sleep, because the change is **far enough off** to plan for.
S4.quote: Nobody wants a robot poking around their fuse box at nine at night, and my uncle Ray has been doing that for thirty years.
fieldNote: She still expects the **buying job to go**, but ten years gives her room to control the switch.
She can't yet explain how she'd **afford an apprenticeship** on thin savings, and admits it.
Her uncle Ray, an electrician, is her **model** for work that lasts.

steps.text: Keep the dry goods buying job at Harbourline for now
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship within two years
Vote for candidates who promise paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest. Two years with three weeks of savings is nothing. What would help is a wage while you retrain, paid for by the firms that save the money, and a union that covers office workers too, not just the floor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame, and it isn't the computers. Nobody asked the buyers at my firm before the new ordering system came in, and nobody will ask us before the next thing comes either.

headlineQuote: Nobody asked the buyers at my firm before the new ordering system came in, and nobody will ask us before the next thing comes either.
portrait: A 27-year-old **junior buyer** of dry goods at a food-service distributor, with about **three weeks** of savings.
She works by **phone and paper notebook**, never uses AI, and already ranks slowest on the new system.
She is worried even in **AI Plateau**, and **panics** at AGI in two years with no plan.
More warning turns her towards a **forklift licence** or an electrical apprenticeship.
She blames firms that change things **without asking workers**, and puts her faith in the **union**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years with three weeks of savings leaves her nothing to work with.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage while retraining**, paid for by the firms that save money from AI.
A **union** that covers office workers as well as the warehouse floor.
